[M0095] MSE- MtBE achieves the highest CE of 99.5% among all MSEs, whereas the DOL/DME electrolyte only realizes a CE of 98.0% (Figures 2g and S12).
[M0097] As shown in Figure 2h, the cell with MSE-MtBE demonstrates slightly lower plating and stripping overpotential and stable cycling for over 600 h at a current density of 1 mA cm−2, whereas the DOL/DME cell failed after 400 h.
MtBE各倍率容量都更高更稳定，返回C/5仍明显较高；除C/2成核下凹外过电位相近
T13仅C/2精确容量和成核变坏，遗漏其他倍率定性及多数过电位相近。

M0180 main p.7
M0181 main p.7
M0182 main p.7
M0183 main p.7

[M0180] MSE-MtBE achieves higher and more stable capacities at all applied rates (from C/10 to C/2), especially at C/2, where it retains a capacity of 781 mA h g−1 (Figure 5b).
[M0181] In contrast, the DOL/DME cell only shows a capacity of 700 mA h g−1 and drops below 550 mA h g−1 after 10 cycles at C/2.
[M0182] Notably, the gap remains significant after the rate changes back to C/5, as the MSE-MtBE cell recovers a capacity of ∼ 850 mA h g−1, while the baseline cell has less than 700 mA h g−1 retained.
[M0183] Additionally, MSE-MtBE shows comparable overpotentials in the voltage profiles except a larger dip at the nucleation point for the rate of C/2 (Figures 5c and S26).
75%DoD前MtBE浓差极化通常稍大，与25%峰值较低/末期较低并存
预测仅峰值和末期改善，遗漏方向随DOD变化的例外。

M0134 main p.5
M0135 main p.5
M0137 main p.5

[M0134] The difference is much smaller in ηconc, as it is only slightly larger in MSE-MtBE before 75% DOD.
[M0135] In fact, the ηconc in MSE- MtBE has a peak value of 44.7 mV at ∼25% DOD, which is lower than that in DOL/DME (47.4 mV).
[M0137] Additionally, during termination of discharge, most of the electrochemically active surface is covered; the MSE-MtBE cell shows significantly lower ηconc compared to the baseline cell, thanks to its better wettability and potentially more uniform deposition in the electrode (Figure S17).
45°C下DD更高LiPS溶解、更快迁移及Li反应引发严重穿梭，使化成充电达不到2.8V
一般M2降低穿梭未覆盖温度触发、化成无法达到截止电压的独有因果。

M0186 main p.7
M0194 main p.8

[M0186] Such conditions facilitate the generation and migration of LiPS, while also intensifying detrimental side reactions with Li metal.
[M0194] From the voltage profile in Figure 5e, the cell never reaches 2.8 V before the time cutoff, likely due to severe LiPS shuttling resulting from higher polysulfide solubility, faster migration, and its faster reaction with Li metal at higher temperatures.
DD正极氧化硫副产物可能来自电解液分解/硫反应或电极串扰，拖慢离子扩散
M7只概括减少有害氧化物，漏其来源与电解液消耗/串扰路径。

M0231 main p.9

[M0229] Additionally, stronger peaks of oxidized sulfur species (─SOx) were detected on the DOL/DME-derived cathode, which may originate from unwanted decomposition of electrolyte components and their reactions with sulfur species.
[M0230] They could also arise from anode-cathode crosstalk owing to the stronger solvating power of the baseline electrolyte.
[M0231] Unlike the case at the anode, these oxidized sulfur species have less benefits at the cathode surface, but leading to more sluggish ion diffusion.

[M0250] To first clarify the spectral evolution during the SRR—particularly the interactions of long-chain LPSs—the optical cell was potentiostatically held at 2.3 V for 5 h until the current decayed below 0.005 C (Figure S26 ) [ 49 ].
[M0256] When the cell is discharged galvanostatically at C/20, the voltage profile displays the classical two-plateau behavior of Li–S systems, representing the sequential conversion of longchain and short- chain LPSs.
[M0257] In BL (Figure 4a ; Figure S27a ), the elemental sulfur peaks (152, 220, 473 cm− 1 ) gradually diminish as discharge proceeds, while new peaks at 453 and 479 cm− 1 appear around a DoD of ∼ 8%, signifying the formation of longchain LPSs.
[M0258] These peaks subsequently vanish near 70% DoD, aligning well with the voltage plateaus corresponding to the stepwise reduction from elemental sulfur to long-chain LPSs, and further to shorter-chain species.
[M0264] The elemental sulfur reduction proceeds more slowly, and the long-chain LPSs peak (456 cm− 1 ) emerges at around DoD of 21%—signif icantly later than in the BL electrolyte (8%)—indicating a weaker solvating environment and slower SRR kinetics induced by 1200ET.
[M0265] Moreover, this long-chain LPSs peak persists only until ∼ 50% DoD before disappearing, further confirming the altered solubility of LPSs in the presence of a weakly solvating cosolvent.

[M0125] Pairing the galvanostatic intermittent titration technique (GITT) with EIS is an effective approach to study cell polarization.[40] By applying this GITT-EIS method to Li || S cells with practical sulfur loading, the overall cell polarization (ηtotal) can be resolved into three contributions: ohmic (ηohm), activation (ηact), and concentration (ηconc) polarizations. ηohm captures ionic resistance in the bulk electrolyte as well as electronic and contact resistances within the electrodes and cell hardware; it can be extracted from the high-frequency intercept on the Nyquist plot. ηact corresponds to the energy barrier of the interfacial charge-transfer process and, together with ηohm, produces the instantaneous voltage jump observed whenever the current is stepped during GITT measurement.
[M0129] The resulting ηohm for the MSE-MtBE cell is slightly greater than the DOL/DME cell due to their ionic conductivity difference, with both cells exhibiting a peak value at the nucleation point (2.81 mV for MSE-MtBE and 2.10 mV for DOL/DME) when LiPS concentration reaches its maximum.
[M0133] The MSE-MtBE cell shows a greater ηact at the Li2S/Li2S2 nucleation point (19.5 mV) compared to the baseline cell (10.4 mV), likely because of reduced LiPS concentration in MSE-MtBE, leading to fewer nuclei and nucleation sites.
[M0135] In fact, the ηconc in MSE- MtBE has a peak value of 44.7 mV at ∼25% DOD, which is lower than that in DOL/DME (47.4 mV).
[M0137] Additionally, during termination of discharge, most of the electrochemically active surface is covered; the MSE-MtBE cell shows significantly lower ηconc compared to the baseline cell, thanks to its better wettability and potentially more uniform deposition in the electrode (Figure S17).

[M0148] Furthermore, to probe the liquid–liquid sulfur conversion kinetics, temperature-dependent EIS spectra were collected on Li2S6 symmetric cells (Figure S19).
[M0150] DRT peaks appearing at intermediate time constants (10−4 to 10−1 s) are attributed to the Rct of the cell, which is an important indicator of the charge-transfer kinetics.[41,42] These Rct values measured between 0 and 50 °C fit well in an Arrhenius plot, from which activation energies were extracted (Figure 3i).
[M0151] Interestingly, the MSE-MtBE cell exhibits higher Rct throughout the temperature range, but a lower activation energy compared to DOL/DME.
[M0152] This suggests that the energy barrier for the charge-transfer process, which is likely associated with desolvation at the electrochemically active surface, is lower in MSE-MtBE, whereas the overall reaction rate is slower, plausibly due to the lower conductivity of MSE-MtBE (Figure S21).

[M0161] Before cycling, both the DOL/DME and MSE-MtBE cells exhibit strong α-S8 signals as expected.
[M0164] Both cells show a complete disappearance of sulfur peaks during discharge, indicating a complete conversion of sulfur, attributed to the optimized spray-dried sulfur composite particles utilized in the cathode.[43] Interestingly, notable differences between the baseline and MSE-MtBE cells were observed after the subsequent charge.
[M0165] For the DOL/DME cell, a group of β-S8 peaks were detected after charge, which aligns well with previous work in the literature utilizing ether-based electrolytes.[44] However, in the MSE-MtBE cell, β-S8 was first formed toward the end of the charge before peaks corresponding to α-S8 appeared.
[M0166] Note that α-S8 tends to form when the reaction kinetics move toward solid-state conversion.[32,45] This two-step sulfur deposition process could be characteristic in the MSE due to lower LiPS solubility and regulated solvation properties.
[M0167] As a kinetically more favorable process, β-S8 is first nucleated from solvated LiPSs, while thermodynamically more stable α-S8 starts to grow when quasi-solid-state reaction kicks in.
[M0168] Additional ex situ XRD results show that this β – α conversion can happen even on immersing the S cathode retrieved from the DOL/DME cell in MSE-MtBE (Figure S23).

[M0203] After cycling the Li || S cells for 30 cycles, Li metal morphology was examined with scanning electron microscopy (SEM).
[M0204] MSE-MtBE enables dense and uniform Li deposition, packed with large grains, suggesting less parasitic side reactions and dendrite formation (Figure S29).
[M0205] In contrast, Li metal cycled in DOL/DME has more cracks and non-uniform surface morphology.
[M0209] To better study the SEI in different electrolytes, Li anodes after 30 cycles were evaluated with xray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS).
[M0227] The S cathode cycled in DOL/DME showcases significantly larger amounts of reduced S species (SB0 and ST−1), corresponding to the inactive material resulting from extensive LiPS generation (Figure 6d).[32,47] By contrast, the MSE-MtBE-derived cathode retains a much higher fraction of elemental sulfur (S0, S 2p3/2 ≈164.5 eV) in the charged state.
[M0232] Finally, the F 1s spectra show a higher Li─F/C─F ratio for the MSE-MtBE cathode, confirming a more inorganic-rich and conductive surface layer (Figure 6e).

[M0043] The amount of reversible Li was found to be 6.3 mAh cm−2, which is 21% less than the theoretical capacity of the pristine 40-μm-thick LMA (8 mAh cm−2) (Figure 1c,d).
[M0044] The reversible capacity remained larger than the discharge capacity of the Li–S battery (3.04 mAh cm−2), confirming that cell capacity is not limited by the remaining capacity of the LMA, consistent with the results reported in previous studies.[9] However, 21% loss in the LMA indicates significant LMA degradation over 46 cycles only, as supported by the thick, porous layer observed in the cross-sectional images of the cycled LMA (Figure 1e).
[M0046] The results revealed that 33% of DME, 49% of DOL, and 2% of TFSI−anions decomposed during the 46 cycles.
[M0048] The remaining amount of electrolyte (1.76 μL mAh−1), estimated from quantitative NMR (QNMR) analysis, was slightly more than that required to fully wet the S cathode and separator (1.57 μL mAh−1) (Note S1 and Table S1, Supporting Information).
[M0050] To confirm whether electrolyte decomposition is responsible for capacity fade, we reassembled a cell with fresh electrolyte and the electrodes of the failed cells and operated this cell.
[M0051] The cell was rejuvenated owing to electrolyte exchange (Figure 1g), which confirms that solvent depletion is responsible for cell degradation.

[S0197] The curves of I-t was deconvoluted into the three electrochemical processes of long-chain LiPSs, mid-chain LiPSs, and Li2S.32 The deposited Li2S capacity in CSA/MeTHF and DD electrolytes are calculated to be 550 mAh g−1 and 292 mAh g−1, respectively, indicating better reversible conversion from LiPSs to Li2S in CSA/MeTHF electrolyte.

[S0203] The fitting I-t curve of the DD electrolyte closely matches the 2DI model, which is consistent with a Li2S growth process controlled by adatom surface,33 leading to premature termination of Li2S deposition and thus the rapid electrode surface passivation.
[S0204] In contrast, the fitting I-t curve of CSA/MeTHF electrolyte follows the 3DP model, implying that Li2S growth is primarily controlled by bulk diffusion of precursors.
[S0207] A distinctive 3D island-like morphology on the carbon fiber (CF) is observed in CSA/MeTHF electrolyte, which could effectively mitigate the cathode passivation and facilitate rapid ion transport, causing in suppressed LiPSs shuttle effect and improved S utilization.
[S0211] The dissolution capacity of Li2S using CSA/MeTHF electrolyte reaches up to 691 mAh g−1, which is higher than that in DD electrolyte (186 mAh g−1).

[M0168] After the DoD of 25%, ηact becomes the dominant polarization in the DD electrolyte (Figures S46c and S48), indicating sluggish conversion kinetics governed by interfacial chemistry.
[M0169] These kinetics are limited not only by the LiPSs maximum concentration but also by the protracted liquid−solid conversion process.
[M0170] Although, for the CSA/ MeTHF electrolyte, the proportion of ηcon exceeds 50% after the DoD of 25%, all three polarization components maintain consistent trends throughout low voltage plateau.
[M0171] This demonstrates that CSA/MeTHF electrolyte induces stable interfacial chemistry that sustains rapid concentration-dominated conversion, particularly for the shorter order LiPSs.32 Thus, these results demonstrate a clear correlation between interfacial chemistry and electrochemical polarization during the 4 M conversion process, highlighting the critical role of electrolyte engineering.

[S0241] X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) analysis of cycled cathodes reveals that using CSA/MeTHF electrolyte produces strong S 2p signals primarily from SO32− species after the first cycle (Figure S41).
[S0242] This SO32−-rich cathode–electrolyte interphase improves ionic conduction and boosts the reversibility of 4M conversion reaction.35 In sharp contrast, the cycled cathode using DD electrolyte exhibits strong characteristic LiPSs peaks (Figure S42), owing to the prematurely formed 2D Li2S layer.
[S0243] This overt discrepancy demonstrates that the interfacial chemistry crucially plays a key role in regulating the balance between high ionic conduction and rapid conversion kinetics during the 4M conversion process.

M0037 main p.2
M0043 main p.2
M0170 main p.10

[M0037] The as-prepared inflammable electrolyte was composed by simply mixing 2 m LiTFSI/DME with TTE in the volume ratio of 1:4 (denoted as TDE, the average LiTFSI concentration is about 0.4 m), it possess both properties of reducing polysulfide shuttling and stabilizing the lithium metal, the inflammable nature of TTE can remarkably improve the safety of lithium–sulfur batteries. the TDE electrolyte coupled with nanoconductive carbon-coated separator (denote as CS separator) enables the bare sulfur cathode–based batteries excellent rate performance of ≈350 mAh g−1 at 4 C, the initial discharge capacity could reach up to 1187 mAh g−1 at the cathode sulfur loading of 4 mg cm−2 (equals to the areal capacity of 6.7 mAh g−1).
[M0043] According to the flame retardant test shows in Figure S1 (Supporting Information), when the volume ratio of TTE in the mixture solvent is higher than 80% (TTE:2 m LiTFSI/DME = 4:1), spray formed by the TDE electrolyte can effectively extinguish the burning paper roll, however, with the volume ratio of inert TTE increasing, the ionic conductivity is decreasing, thus the volume ratio of TTE: 2 m LiTFSI/ DME = 4:1 is chosen for the flame retardant TDE electrolyte (the concentration of LiNO3 in the TDE electrolyte is around 0.025 m).
[M0170] Preparation Methods—Preparation of TDE Electrolyte: TDE electrolyte was obtained by simply mixing the TTE and 2 m LiTFSI/DME (with 0.1 m LiNO3) electrolyte in 4:1 by volume.

[M0041] To elucidate further on this, we here employ radical traps and pri­ marily operando Raman spectroscopy to directly monitor the effect of S•− 3 on the Li–S battery capacity and cycling stability, using two different electrolytes: 1 M LiTFSI in either DME:DOL or TMU:DOL.
[M0050] Two, 5,5-dimethyl-1-pyrroline-N-oxide (DMPO) and alpha-(4-Pyridyl N-oxide)-N-tert-butylnitrone (PotBN), are widely used as nitrone radical traps, while the other two are ionic liquids (ILs) 1-ethyl-3-methyl-imidazolium bis(trifluoromethylsulfonyl)imide and 1-butyl-3-methyl-pyridinium bis(trifluoromethylsulfonyl)imide, which, for simplicity, henceforth will be referred to as Emim and BmPyr, respec­ tively (Fig.
[M0069] Two electrolytes were used without and with four different traps (Emim, PotBN, DMPO and BmPyr): 1 M LiTFSI in DME: DOL (1:1, v:v) and 1 M LiTFSI in TMU: DOL (1:1, v:v).
[M0070] The quantity of trap in the electrolyte was equivalent to 0.78 mmol of nitrone/or imi­ nium cation in 1 ml of electrolyte, which is 3.1 10−2 mmol/mgS nitrone/ or iminium cation to sulfur ratio.
[M0099] Please first note that, as opposed to what usually is the case, no LiNO3 was added to the electrolyte, in order to avoid any possible interaction with S•− 3 , and this explains the incomplete charge potential (due to PSs shuttling).

[M0033] Li+ interacts with S82− tightly both in DOL/DME and HFE-EPSE, implying the dissociation of Li2S8 is weak (Figure 1a,d).[22] In DOL/ DME, DME emerges at 4.4 Å from the center of S82− through S82−–Li+–solvent interactions and the inner solvent shell (shell 1) is formed.
[M0034] Following DME, DOL appears at 6.6 Å to form the outer solvent shell (shell 2).
[M0036] The introduction of HFE into DOL/DME dramatically changes the LiPS outer solvent shell other than the inner solvent shell.
[M0037] Specifically, the inner solvent shell around LiPSs consists of DME (4.4 Å), which is similar to that in DOL/DME to ensure suitable dissolution of LiPSs.[23] HFE emerges at 6.4 Å which is recruited in the second solvent shell (Figure 1d).
[M0040] Considering that solvents interact with LiPSs by S82−–Li+–solvent interactions,[22] 7Li-NMR was used to infer the distribution of solvents around LiPSs. 1.0 m [S] Li2S8 dissolving in DOL/DME or HFE-EPSE is chosen as the electrolyte to imitate the electrolyte formulation used in MD simulations.
[M0041] The chemical shift of 7Li is 3.20 ppm both for DOL/DME and HFE-EPSE, indicating HFE barely interacts with Li+ and does not change the inner solvent shell of LiPSs (Figure 1g).
[M0044] The signal of polysulfides (392, 448, and 510 cm−1), DME (845 cm−1), and DOL (945 cm−1) nearly overlaps for DOL/DME and HFE-EPSE,[24] indicating the inner solvent shell around LiPSs maintains with the introduction of HFE (Figure 1h and Figure S1, Supporting Information).
[M0045] A similar conclusion is obtained for 1.0 m [S] Li2S6 (Figures S2 and S3, Supporting Information).

[M0127] In stage II, with insufficient SSSs for full coordination of LiPSs and increased molecular entropy, the WSSs begin to enter the inner solvation shell and directly coordinate with LiPSs following the Li bond principle.60 These changes in the LiPS solvation structure induced by WSS coordination result in a two-stage variation in the ESP and further affect the LiPS kinetic behaviors in Li−S batteries.

[M0028] A key observation from the CID spectra of different lithiated adducts (Figure 1 and Table 1) is that 2FPy has a stronger interaction with Li+ than 3FPy when both are referenced to a pyridine solvent.
[M0029] According to calculations by Choi et al.,25 the DNs for 2FPy and 3FPy are 15.8 and 29.7 kcal mol−1, respectively, suggesting that 3FPy should exhibit a stronger interaction with Li+ than 2FPy.
[M0030] However, this prediction is inconsistent with the CID data (Table 1), which shows that a relative abundance of [2FPy + Li]+ is 55.1% (compared to the abundance of [Py + Li]+) and the relative abundance of [3FPy + Li]+ is only 9.6%.
[M0032] This insight may explain the stronger interaction of Li+ with 2FPy.
[M0033] In 2FPy, the fluorine atom is positioned close to the nitrogen atom in the pyridine ring, possibly enhancing the Li+ interaction with nitrogen through a synergistic effect, even though fluorine’s electron-withdrawing nature slightly reduces the electron density on nitrogen (Scheme S-1).
[M0034] In contrast, the fluorine atom in 3FPy is positioned farther from the nitrogen atom in pyridine, lacking this synergistic effect.
[M0093] CID spectra revealed that Li+ exhibits preferential solvation in different fluoropyridines, with 2FPy showing a stronger interaction with Li+ than 4FPy and 3FPy, likely due to the ortho-fluorine interaction unique to 2FPy.

[M0073] It is well established that in pyridine rings, nucleophilic aromatic substitution primarily occurs at the ortho (o) or para (p) position, while electrophilic substitution typically targets the meta (m) position.31 Although fluorine substitution in the pyridine ring may reduce the reactivity of 2FPy, the nucleophilic substitution of fluorine cannot be entirely prevented when strong nucleophiles, such as polysulfides, are present.
[M0074] The presence of Py-S-CH3 and Py-S2-CH3 in the HPLC chromatogram provides evidence for the formation of Py-S−and Py-S2 −, which are likely products of the nucleophilic substitution reaction between 2FPy and polysulfides.

[M0077] According to the prior research on organodisulfides (e.g., dipyridyl disulfides) by Fu et al.,32 this small discharge plateau above 2.4 V likely results from organosulfide species formed through the ongoing reactions between 2FPy and polysulfides during the cycling.

[M0125] The transition dividing stage I and stage II depends on whether the WSS enters the LiPS inner solvation shell.
[M0127] In stage II, with insufficient SSSs for full coordination of LiPSs and increased molecular entropy, the WSSs begin to enter the inner solvation shell and directly coordinate with LiPSs following the Li bond principle.60 These changes in the LiPS solvation structure induced by WSS coordination result in a two-stage variation in the ESP and further affect the LiPS kinetic behaviors in Li−S batteries.
[M0150] The above results manifest that the chargetransfer kinetics of the LiPS homogeneous reactions become intrinsically more sluggish with reduced ESP once the WSSs penetrate the LiPS inner solvation shell.
[M0165] Overall, based on the experimental and theoretical evaluations of both homogeneous and heterogeneous reactions, it is evident that direct coordination of WSS with LiPSs significantly lessens the ESP of the WSEs, which further reduces the intrinsic LiPS reactivity, hinders the cathodic charge-transfer kinetics, and sharply enlarges the cathodic activation polarization.

[M0125] Pairing the galvanostatic intermittent titration technique (GITT) with EIS is an effective approach to study cell polarization.[40] By applying this GITT-EIS method to Li || S cells with practical sulfur loading, the overall cell polarization (ηtotal) can be resolved into three contributions: ohmic (ηohm), activation (ηact), and concentration (ηconc) polarizations. ηohm captures ionic resistance in the bulk electrolyte as well as electronic and contact resistances within the electrodes and cell hardware; it can be extracted from the high-frequency intercept on the Nyquist plot. ηact corresponds to the energy barrier of the interfacial charge-transfer process and, together with ηohm, produces the instantaneous voltage jump observed whenever the current is stepped during GITT measurement.
[M0129] The resulting ηohm for the MSE-MtBE cell is slightly greater than the DOL/DME cell due to their ionic conductivity difference, with both cells exhibiting a peak value at the nucleation point (2.81 mV for MSE-MtBE and 2.10 mV for DOL/DME) when LiPS concentration reaches its maximum.
[M0133] The MSE-MtBE cell shows a greater ηact at the Li2S/Li2S2 nucleation point (19.5 mV) compared to the baseline cell (10.4 mV), likely because of reduced LiPS concentration in MSE-MtBE, leading to fewer nuclei and nucleation sites.
[M0135] In fact, the ηconc in MSE- MtBE has a peak value of 44.7 mV at ∼25% DOD, which is lower than that in DOL/DME (47.4 mV).
[M0137] Additionally, during termination of discharge, most of the electrochemically active surface is covered; the MSE-MtBE cell shows significantly lower ηconc compared to the baseline cell, thanks to its better wettability and potentially more uniform deposition in the electrode (Figure S17).

[M0161] Before cycling, both the DOL/DME and MSE-MtBE cells exhibit strong α-S8 signals as expected.
[M0164] Both cells show a complete disappearance of sulfur peaks during discharge, indicating a complete conversion of sulfur, attributed to the optimized spray-dried sulfur composite particles utilized in the cathode.[43] Interestingly, notable differences between the baseline and MSE-MtBE cells were observed after the subsequent charge.
[M0165] For the DOL/DME cell, a group of β-S8 peaks were detected after charge, which aligns well with previous work in the literature utilizing ether-based electrolytes.[44] However, in the MSE-MtBE cell, β-S8 was first formed toward the end of the charge before peaks corresponding to α-S8 appeared.
[M0166] Note that α-S8 tends to form when the reaction kinetics move toward solid-state conversion.[32,45] This two-step sulfur deposition process could be characteristic in the MSE due to lower LiPS solubility and regulated solvation properties.
[M0167] As a kinetically more favorable process, β-S8 is first nucleated from solvated LiPSs, while thermodynamically more stable α-S8 starts to grow when quasi-solid-state reaction kicks in.
[M0168] Additional ex situ XRD results show that this β – α conversion can happen even on immersing the S cathode retrieved from the DOL/DME cell in MSE-MtBE (Figure S23).

[M0038] Failure Analysis of a Lean-Electrolyte Li–S Battery The root cause of the degradation of lean-electrolyte Li–S batteries was re-examined at an E/S ratio of 5 using 1 m lithium bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl)imide (LiTFSI), 0.2 m LiNO3, and DME/DOL (1:1 v/v), which is considered to be a baseline electrolyte for Li–S batteries.[2] As shown in Figure 1a, operating the cell at a 0.15 C discharge/charge rate significantly declines the discharge capacity after 40 cycles.
[M0039] At the 46th cycle, an abnormal-shaped, fluctuating second voltage plateau appeared, indicating cell failure (Figure 1b).
[M0043] The amount of reversible Li was found to be 6.3 mAh cm−2, which is 21% less than the theoretical capacity of the pristine 40-μm-thick LMA (8 mAh cm−2) (Figure 1c,d).
[M0044] The reversible capacity remained larger than the discharge capacity of the Li–S battery (3.04 mAh cm−2), confirming that cell capacity is not limited by the remaining capacity of the LMA, consistent with the results reported in previous studies.[9] However, 21% loss in the LMA indicates significant LMA degradation over 46 cycles only, as supported by the thick, porous layer observed in the cross-sectional images of the cycled LMA (Figure 1e).
[M0046] The results revealed that 33% of DME, 49% of DOL, and 2% of TFSI−anions decomposed during the 46 cycles.
[M0048] The remaining amount of electrolyte (1.76 μL mAh−1), estimated from quantitative NMR (QNMR) analysis, was slightly more than that required to fully wet the S cathode and separator (1.57 μL mAh−1) (Note S1 and Table S1, Supporting Information).
[M0050] To confirm whether electrolyte decomposition is responsible for capacity fade, we reassembled a cell with fresh electrolyte and the electrodes of the failed cells and operated this cell.
[M0051] The cell was rejuvenated owing to electrolyte exchange (Figure 1g), which confirms that solvent depletion is responsible for cell degradation.

[M0148] The obtained sulfur loading was 1.1–1.3 mg cm−2, and 2.01 cm2 cathode disks were used.
[M0152] To assemble CR2032-type coin cells, metallic lithium anode (2.01 cm2, 170 μm) and polymeric Celgard (3.01 cm2, 25 μm) separators were used under an inert atmosphere.
[M0153] Cells with different E/S ratios of 6, 9, 16, and 23 mL g−1 were prepared for different types of electrolytes, keeping other parameters such as the sulfur loading and carbon-to-sulfur ratio constant.
[M0154] The prepared cells were kept at the open circuit voltage (OCV) for 16 h for stabilization.
[M0155] Galvanostatic cycling was carried out at room temperature by a Neware battery cycler.
[M0156] After resting, each cell was cycled at 0.1 Crate between cut-off voltages of 1.5–2.8 V.
[M0158] Then, at the end of the rest period and the end of the first, third, fifth, eighth, and tenth discharge, the EIS measurements were conducted within 10 mHz to 1 MHz, with a 10 mV amplitude using Biologic SP 300/300e.
[M0160] In the EIS characterization, the lowest E/S ratio, 6 mL g−1, was chosen since we are particularly interested in low E/S ratios for practical Li-S batteries.
[M0162] CV analysis was performed between 1.5 and 3.0 V with a scan rate of 0.1 mV s−1 by using Biologic SP 300/300e.
